doc.title: David Finck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 29, 2015

title: Wishing for an earlier era and the state of the business
summary: Finck wishes he had worked in 1960s-70s New York and says recording sessions have declined.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Wow. Do you ever — sometimes I’m fascinated about living in another era. And I wonder if you ever have done that? For musical reasons?

Yeah. Every now and then I wish I had been maybe a generation and a half or two generations before. I think before the music business went digital and there were some players that I would have loved to have the opportunity to work with. So yeah, once in a while. I suppose everybody does. And of course business-wise all the guys a generation or two older than me go, “oh yeah, you should have been in New York in the 1960’s through ’79.” Because there were more jobs than there were players.
They were doing three dates a day.
But you know it looks like you’re busy to me. From what I’ve read about you. Is that a fair statement?

I would say generally I am, but our business is affected by the economy. And usually the first thing to go — nobody’s going to eliminate the flow of oil and gas and electricity. But they can do without entertainment if they have to. So I would say now there seem to be fewer and fewer recording sessions, although I’ve been producing records for people and I do my best to do it all with live musicians. And the guys really — we always have a good time. They go, “oh man, this is like the old days. It’s actually a big band.” Or, “man, I remember when we used to do this twice a week.” And I think for that reason, because they are live players I think the records sound really good.
